headlines.summary: Microsoft is trying to balance a rapid infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
headlines.article_text: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Around 60,000 Microsoft employees are eligible for the new buyout program across four countries, said a person familiar with the matter. The move comes six months after Microsoft announced its first-ever voluntary retirement program to a small set of U.S. workers. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31. In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Pedestrians walk past a Microsoft office in New York, US, on Tuesday, July 22, 2025. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty Images Microsoft said Monday that it is offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance an artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency. The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below. Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people. Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. That put a strain on Microsoft's finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees . "The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees . "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program." In the second quarter, Microsoft's cloud rivals, Alphabet and Amazon, both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year. Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added. Over 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July . But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around. On Wednesday Microsoft reports third-quarter results. headlines.article_text: Anthropic IPO live updates: AI lab's S-1 filing Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 1:57 01:57 Anthropic lost $80.7 billion in the first half of this year: What you need to know Squawk on the Street Anthropic is officially headed for the public market in what is expected to be a historic offering for a 5-year-old company that's been at the heart of the generative artificial intelligence boom. In a Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission , Anthropic said it plans to list on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol "ANT." The company behind Claude confidentially filed with the SEC in June, giving the agency time to review its financials before they were made available to the public and prospective investors. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic's Claude model and services have captivated the corporate world, as companies have opened their wallets in an effort to crack new growth opportunities and find internal efficiencies. Expansion has accelerated in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of AI coding tool Claude Code , and powerful models including Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 . The company has been racing to maintain an edge over competitors like OpenAI and Google , and faced sharp criticism over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government in recent months. Anthropic's offering, if it doesn't get derailed, will land just a few months after Elon Musk's SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion. It's been a volatile stretch for SpaceX shares, which finished last week slightly below where they opened in June. As it prepares to hit the market, Anthropic has to contend with severe jitters on Wall Street as concerns grow over whether spending on AI services will justify the trillions of dollars in expected infrastructure costs. So-called neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius have been hammered of late, losing over 30% of their value in October as credit risk is rising across the data center space. What you need to know about the IPO: Alphabet set to be a bigger shareholder More than 90 pages of risk factors OpenAI and Google listed as the competition How Anthropic's "Founder LLC" voting power works Here's what Anthropic's top execs get paid Billions in commitments with Microsoft Anthropic reports $80.7 billion loss in first half of 2026 Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters CNBC's reporters are covering Anthropic's IPO from bureaus in San Francisco and Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey. 9 Min Ago Anthropic uses AI chips from Nvidia, AMD, Amazon and Google Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., shows Vera Rubin computer modules during the keynote address at the Nvidia GTC in Berlin, Germany, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Alex Kraus | Bloomberg | Getty Images Anthropic said its pool of computing power includes Nvidia's GPUs, AMD's GPUs, AWS Tranium, and Google TPUs. Anthropic treats all AI chips as a "single fungible pool" and it has developed technology that routes its AI models to whatever chip is the most efficient at the time. It's a sign that Anthropic won't tie itself to any one chip provider. OpenAI, which mostly uses Nvidia compute, has made similar moves to diversify the AI chips it uses. "Our multi-chip compute approach provides us with substantially greater chip access than relying on one platform and enables us to opportunistically capture the price-performance benefits of each chip family and generation," Anthropic said in its filing. All four of Anthropic's primary chip designers have large stakes or options to buy stakes in Anthropic, highlighting the strategic ties between chipmakers or hyperscalers and the AI labs. Anthropic's filing left the amount of total money it has committed to spending on compute blank, but the frontier lab signaled it will spend heavily. Separately, Anthropic detailed long-term commitments with SpaceXAI, Nscale, and Lambda to secure access to Nvidia chips. The company also said it could buy more than $20 billion in AMD chips. It said it was committed to spending on Amazon's Trainium chips at $110 billion through 2036, and $114.5 billion on Google TPUs through 2033. "We anticipate making significant investments for the foreseeable future, including in compute and infrastructure, to ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the frontier of AI," Anthropic said in the filing. — Kif Leswing 17 Min Ago Anthropic's implied gross margins have exploded, but cost of compute may change that Anthropic reported its cost of revenue as $2.38 billion as of June 30, 2026, booking $16.29 billion in revenue during the same period and implying a gross margin of 85%. That's an explosion from the implied 12% gross margin the company generated during the same period last year, on just over $1 billion in cost of revenue and $1.16 billion in revenue booked. However, Anthropic's S-1 states that operating margin and adjusted operating margin are expected to "fluctuate over time, particularly in periods when substantial incremental compute is delivered to us and we incur the associated expenses." The prospectus also reveals that "substantially all of cost of revenue" is associated with compute and infrastructure costs, adding that smaller personnel and overhead-related costs are also factored in. —Isabel O'Brien 22 Min Ago Amazon's deepening ties to Anthropic Amazon's largest AI data center has seven completed buildings, with 30 total buildings planned on 1,200 acres in New Carlisle, Indiana, shown here on October 8, 2025. Erin Black Amazon remains one of Anthropic's biggest backers and strategic partners. The company has poured $13 billion into Anthropic since 2023 , with the potential to invest $20 billion more. According to the filing, Amazon has separately agreed to provide up to $15 billion in financing, which will become available to Anthropic in $5 billion tranches. Each draw is tied to Anthropic hitting certain compute capacity milestones. Amazon holds $6.2 billion in outstanding convertible notes that could be worth $1.84 billion once Anthropic goes public. Amazon's stake is capped at 12% of the company, the filing states. Amazon holds nonvoting shares and it doesn't have a board or observer seat at the startup. The companies have continued to deepen their partnership, with Anthropic becoming a key customer of Amazon's cloud computing and chips businesses. Amazon last year opened an $11 billion AI data center campus dedicated to training and running models from Anthropic, called Rainier. In April, Anthropic said it committed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon for cloud services through April 2036, "regardless of actual usage." The agreement is "non-cancelable," except for in the event of a "material breach" by Amazon, the filing says. If Anthropic's actual spend falls short, it's required to pay Amazon the difference as a true-up. The filing doesn't state how much Anthropic has spent on Amazon's cloud services and Trainium AI chips to date. — Annie Palmer 35 Min Ago Anthropic H1 2026 overseas revenue tops $4.5 billion amid global expansion Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic, at the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, India, on Thursday, Feb. 19, 2026. headlines.article_text: Apollo nears deal for 10% Mubadala Capital stake Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apollo is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, according to people familiar with the matter; the transaction has not yet been publicly announced. Mubadala Capital is the alternative asset management subsidiary of Abu Dhabi sovereign investor Mubadala Investment Co. Mubadala Capital says it manages, advises and administers more than $755 billion, while its wholly owned core alternatives businesses manage and invest more than $60 billion. In this article APO Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 5:17 05:17 Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital Squawk Box Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity. The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known. The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership. Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide. In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon. For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion. Apollo Global Management, YTD John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever. "Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal. Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision. Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco. Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement. Goldman Sachs estimates that artificial intelligence-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031. In this article NVDA AMD AVGO META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintelligence. The stock was down 1.6% in morning trading after the announcement. Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement. The tech giant will initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program. The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure build-out. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power. Meta's planned investments will support "emerging AI opportunities" including its family of apps, its AI agent Muse and its data center business, the company said Monday. It plans to balance funding for these investments through a mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and equity capital. Meta racing to secure AI infrastructure Meta is among the major hyperscalers that are increasingly tapping debt to fund the expensive infrastructure required for the AI boom. Last week, Meta posted third-quarter results showing revenue jumped 26% year on year: $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. However, investors focused more on the tech company's negative free cash flow and its higher full-year capital expenditure forecast. It now expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. That sent Meta's shares lower on Thursday. Meta is building four "superclusters" with more than 1 gigawatt of capacity each and is on track to nearly double total infrastructure capacity in 2026 on a year-over-year basis, the company said. The decision to raise more money "reflects the eye-watering levels of investment required to keep up in the AI arms race," Ben Wood, senior partner at CCS Insight, told CNBC. "Meta offering more stock comes at a time when numerous companies, such as Google, SpaceX and soon, Anthropic, are going to the markets to raise funds." Alphabet, Google's parent company, said it would look to raise $85 billion in June. SpaceX has closed a $40 billion debt financing to purchase graphics processing units. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering. TikTok U.S. is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity over the coming years, CNBC reported Friday.
